title: Desk Lamp
hook: Its springs balance the head’s weight at every angle, so the arm stays wherever you let it go.
summary: A desk lamp has to put its light anywhere within reach and stay there, without a knob to tighten at every joint. George Carwardine’s answer, patented in 1932, was a spring whose pull grows with its whole length, hung from a point straight above each pivot. Its torque then rises and falls with the arm’s angle exactly as the weight’s does, and the two cancel everywhere.

The head hangs on a bracket at the end of the upper arm, two bars that make a parallelogram and keep it at one angle. Two springs from a pin above the elbow pivot answer the upper arm. The elbow plates are the far side of a second parallelogram, the lower arm and its parallel link, so they never turn; two more springs from a pin above the shoulder answer everything above it, and the clamp takes it all into the desk.

Move the head and each arm turns about its pin while its springs stretch or shorten, storing exactly the energy the head gives up. Here each arm moves in turn and its springs stretch or shorten with it, worked out from the same numbers. The masses are estimates and the springs ideal, and the model’s two parallelograms were trued by up to 5 mm.

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 89 cm tall, 61 cm deep as posed

facts.label: Arms
facts.value: 442 mm and 464 mm, pin to pin

parts.label: Shade
parts.about: A steel cone that throws the light down and keeps it out of your eyes. Its own knuckle on the bracket tilts it and holds it by friction: the one joint here that friction does hold.

parts.label: Bulb
parts.about: A pear-shaped E27 bulb, a few tens of grams of the head’s 0.4 kg (an estimate).

parts.label: Lamp holder
parts.about: The E27 holder the bulb screws into. Its cable loops out of the shade’s back and along the arm.

parts.label: Head bracket
parts.about: Two plates pinned to both upper bars. The bars stay parallel, so the bracket shifts as the arm moves but never turns: the head keeps the angle you gave it.

parts.label: Upper bar
parts.about: The lower of the upper arm’s two bars, 464 mm pin to pin. It turns about the elbow pin, and the upper springs pull on a pin 218 mm along it.

parts.label: Upper link
parts.about: The upper bar’s partner, pinned 36 mm above it at both ends. The two make a parallelogram that carries the head level.

parts.label: Upper spring, left
parts.about: One of the upper pair: from the pin 36.3 mm straight above the elbow pivot to the pin 218 mm along the upper bar. Wound with initial tension, it pulls in proportion to its whole length.

parts.label: Upper spring, right
parts.about: The other of the upper pair. Between them they pull with 293 N for every metre of their length: 57 N as modelled.

parts.label: Elbow plates
parts.about: The plates that join the arms. They’re the far side of the lower parallelogram, so they never turn, and the upper springs’ anchor stays straight above the elbow pivot.

parts.label: Lower arm
parts.about: Two side bars, 442 mm from the shoulder pin to the elbow. Everything above the elbow, about 0.7 kg, hangs on its far end.

parts.label: Parallel link
parts.about: A bar the same length as the lower arm, pinned to the base bracket and the elbow plates. It keeps the plates from turning as the lower arm moves.

parts.label: Lower spring, left
parts.about: One of the lower pair: from a pin 65.7 mm straight above the shoulder pin to the pin 216 mm along the lower arm.

parts.label: Lower spring, right
parts.about: The other of the lower pair. Between them they pull with 270 N for every metre of their length: 46 N as modelled.

parts.label: Base bracket
parts.about: The fixed side of the lower parallelogram: it carries the shoulder pin, the parallel link’s pin and the lower springs’ anchors, and turns on the clamp.

parts.label: Clamp
parts.about: A screw clamp for the desk’s edge. The springs’ pull and the lamp’s weight go into the desk here.

parts.label: Clamp screw
parts.about: Turned up under the desk by its tommy bar, it squeezes the desk top against the clamp’s upper jaw.

annotations.title: The load
annotations.text: The head (shade, bulb and holder) weighs about 0.4 kg and hangs 464 mm out from the elbow. Its pull about the elbow pin is 2.32 N·m times the sine of the upper arm’s angle from upright: nothing standing up, most lying level.

annotations.title: A head that keeps its angle
annotations.text: The upper arm is two bars pinned 36 mm apart at both ends, a parallelogram, so the head bracket shifts but never turns. Move the arm and the light still points the way you aimed it.

annotations.title: Upper springs
annotations.text: Two springs from a pin straight above the elbow pivot to a pin 218 mm along the upper bar. Their torque about the elbow is k × 36.3 mm × 218 mm × sin ψ; at 293 N/m that is 2.32 N·m × sin ψ, the weight’s own curve.

annotations.title: Pull in proportion to length
annotations.text: The springs are wound with initial tension: their coils stay pressed together until pulled as hard as their rate times their closed length. Past that, the pull is proportional to the whole length, as if the spring could shorten to nothing. An ordinary spring of the same rate would hold under half the weight.

annotations.title: Elbow plates that never turn
annotations.text: The elbow plates are the far side of the lower parallelogram (lower arm, parallel link, base bracket), so they move but never turn. That keeps the upper springs’ anchor straight above the elbow pivot, as the balance needs, whatever the lower arm does.

annotations.title: Lower springs
annotations.text: Two springs from a pin 65.7 mm above the shoulder pivot to a pin 216 mm along the lower arm. They answer everything above the shoulder, 3.83 N·m × sin θ, with 270 N/m between them.

annotations.title: Not friction
annotations.text: The joints aren’t stiff: the springs carry the whole weight at every angle, and the pins turn freely. Held by friction alone, the shoulder would need to grip with up to 3.8 N·m, and you’d fight that grip every time you moved the lamp.

annotations.title: Into the desk
annotations.text: The bracket turns on the clamp, and the screw squeezes the desk top between the jaws. The springs’ pull and the lamp’s weight both end here.

film.caption: Push the head out and the lower springs stretch, pulling harder just as the weight does.
Lift the head and the upper springs shorten, easing off just as the weight’s pull does.
Let go and it stays put: at every angle the springs answer the weight exactly.

credit.title: Desk Lamp Arm 01
credit.author: Kuutti Siitonen (modelling and texturing) & Yann Kervran (rigging)

extra.label: Changed for this site
extra.text: Cut into its links and pinned to move; the springs rebuilt as coils that stretch; both parallelograms trued (pins moved up to 5 mm). Balance after G. Carwardine, GB 404,615 (1932), and M. J. French & M. B. Widden (2000); masses estimated.
